messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
- Failing test: DiscreteRealDistributionTest.testIssue942 constructs a DiscreteDistribution<Object> with two entries:
  - First key: new Object() {} (an anonymous subclass of Object) with probability 0.
  - Second key: new Object() {} (a different anonymous subclass) with probability 1.
  It then calls sample(1) and asserts the returned array has length 1.

- Relevant code:
  - DiscreteDistribution.sample(int):
    - Creates the result array with:
      T[] out = (T[]) Array.newInstance(singletons.get(0).getClass(), sampleSize);
    - Fills it with:
      out[i] = sample();
  - DiscreteDistribution.sample():
    - Draws according to probabilities and returns the corresponding singleton from the list.

- What happens in the test:
  - Because the first entry has probability 0 and the second has probability 1, sample() will always return the second element.
  - The array created in sample(int) uses the runtime class of the first singleton as its component type (the anonymous class of the first new Object() {}).
  - The second singleton is of a different anonymous subclass type. When the code executes out[0] = sample(), the JVM attempts to store an instance of the second anonymous subclass into an array whose component type is the first anonymous subclass. This is not allowed and results in an ArrayStoreException at line 190.

- Alignment with the current bug report:
  - The report warns that using Array.newInstance(singletons.get(0).getClass(), sampleSize) is unsafe if the first element is of a subclass T1 but sample() returns an element of another type T (not T1). This exactly matches the failure: both keys are different subclasses of Object; the array is built for the first subclass but receives an element of the second subclass.

- Root cause:
  - sample(int) assumes all sampled values are instances of the exact same runtime class as the first singleton. This assumption breaks when the distribution holds heterogeneous runtime types (even if they share a common supertype T), leading to ArrayStoreException during assignment.

- Why the assertion is never reached:
  - The exception is thrown before returning from sample(1), so the test fails prior to checking the array length.

In summary, DiscreteDistribution.sample(int) incorrectly constructs the result array using the first singleton’s runtime class, which can be incompatible with other sampled values. This causes an ArrayStoreException in scenarios like the test, where the first and sampled elements are different subclasses.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
